definition: Breaking down text into smaller parts, like words or characters, to help a computer understand the language.
Converting words or sentences into numbers (vectors) so a computer can process them to find patterns and relationships.
The text or instructions you give to an LLM. It tells the model what you want it to do or answer.
The maximum amount of text (tokens) an LLM can consider at once. Like how much the model can 'remember' in a single conversation.
Training an existing model on new data so it gets better at specific tasks or styles without starting from scratch.
When the model generates a response based on your input. It uses what it learned to produce text, one token at a time.
A type of neural network architecture that uses attention to process sequences of data. Most modern LLMs are built on transformers.
A mechanism that lets the model focus on the most relevant parts of the input when generating each part of the output.
Large Language Model. A type of AI trained on huge amounts of text to understand and generate human-like language.
A setting that controls how random or predictable the model's responses are. Higher values mean more variety; lower values mean more focused, repeatable answers.
